config.title: Two of Everything in Berlin - FAQ
config.subtitle: Why the divided city ended up with duplicate zoos, opera houses and stations, which twin is worth your afternoon, and which pairs the reunified city has already settled for you.

items.q: Why does Berlin have two zoos, two opera houses and two planetariums?
items.a: **Because for forty years it was two cities, and neither half was willing to go without.** Zoo Berlin, opened in 1844, ended up in the British sector, so the GDR built the **Tierpark** in Friedrichsfelde in 1955. The **Deutsche Oper** opened on Bismarckstrasse on 24 September 1961, six weeks after the Wall went up, because the **Staatsoper Unter den Linden** was now on the other side. The pattern repeats across concert halls, libraries, universities and planetariums.

items.q: Which side of Berlin should I actually spend my day on?
items.a: **The eastern side, on a first visit.** Museum Island, the Staatsoper, the Konzerthaus, the Rotes Rathaus, Humboldt-Universitaet and the Fernsehturm sit inside a fifteen minute walk of each other. The western twins are scattered from Charlottenburg to Dahlem, and reaching them costs a U-Bahn ride each time. Pick one side per day and group the outliers at the start or the end.

items.q: Is the Funkturm worth visiting if I have already been up the Fernsehturm?
items.a: **Yes, and it is the better photograph.** The **Funkturm** is West Berlin's 1926 answer to a landmark tower, out at the Messe grounds in Charlottenburg. Its platform is at **126 m**, against 203 m at the Fernsehturm, but it is open **Tuesday to Sunday, 11:00 to 21:00**, it is cheap, and it is usually almost empty. From up there the Fernsehturm is the thing on the horizon.

items.q: What can I actually see at Rathaus Schoeneberg?
items.a: **The balcony where Kennedy said Ich bin ein Berliner in June 1963, and the Freedom Bell above it.** Rathaus Schoeneberg was West Berlin's seat of government from 1949 until 1991, and the bell in the tower, paid for by American donations in 1950, still **rings at noon every day**. Arrive just before twelve, at U4 Rathaus Schoeneberg, or the trip is only a building.

items.q: Are the two main stations and the old airports still in use?
items.a: **No, both of those pairs are settled.** Bahnhof Zoo was West Berlin's long-distance terminus and Ostbahnhof carried the name Hauptbahnhof from 1987, and both lost their intercity trains when **Berlin Hauptbahnhof** opened in May 2006. **Tempelhof** closed in 2008, **Tegel** in 2020, and the eastern airport at Schoenefeld ran on as BER's Terminal 5 until it closed for good in 2022. Book to Hauptbahnhof, and fly into BER in the far south east.

items.q: Where can I see the old border without going to the Wall memorial?
items.a: **Between any pair on the map.** The line between the Philharmonie and the Konzerthaus is about 1.5 km and crosses what was the deadliest strip of the city. The **Staatsbibliothek** is the clearest case of all: one library in two houses, at Unter den Linden and on Potsdamer Strasse, because the collection was split in 1945 and never fully put back together.
